title: Needle-felted alpaca
subtitle: A fluffy long-necked alpaca in cream or fawn merino
excerpt: Needle felt a compact alpaca with its characteristic long neck, small head, and fluffy fibre coat. The finished alpaca is about 9 cm tall. The neck-to-body join is the key construction point; getting it right gives the piece its distinctive silhouette.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from traditional needle-felting guild practice. Alpaca forms are a popular beginner subject, particularly in crafting communities with connections to small-scale fibre animal keeping.

glossaryTerms.definition: A dry felting method using barbed needles to lock wool fibres together without heat or water.
Wool drawn into a continuous ribbon; the standard input material for needle-felting work.

content.text: is a round body set on four slender legs with a long, upright neck and a small head at the top. The head is tiny relative to the body, much smaller than a horse or cow proportionally, and the ears are upright and pointed. Use cream or fawn
for the body. A shallow-angle surface pass on the finished body suggests the fluffy alpaca fleece without over-complicating the construction.

attrs.title: Needle safety
attrs.body: Stab straight in and out at 90 degrees. Keep the finger guard on the supporting hand at all times.

items.name: Cream, fawn, or caramel merino roving
Dark brown or black merino roving (face markings, hooves)
Strong thread and needle for bead eyes

content.text: Roll a generous amount of fawn roving into a compact oval body about 5 cm long and 4 cm across. Needle felt on all sides until firm. The alpaca body is compact and round; resist lengthening it. Leave the bottom flat so the alpaca will stand on its legs.

Roll four sausages of fawn roving, each about 3 cm long and about 7 mm thick when firm. Needle felt each leg solid. Attach two legs at the front underside of the body and two at the rear, pressing each one firmly against the body and needling through the join from all sides. Stand the body on the four legs and check that it is stable before proceeding; adjust leg angles if needed by bending the base of each leg slightly before it is fully locked.

Roll a sausage of fawn roving about 4 cm long and 1 cm thick when firm; the neck is noticeably long and slender in alpacas. Needle it to a firm cylinder, then attach it upright at the front centre of the body. Needle firmly through the neck base into the body from front and back and both sides to lock the joint.

Roll a small oval head, about 2 cm long, and needle it firmly. Attach it to the top of the neck. The head sits forward of vertical on the neck. Alpacas carry their heads slightly out in front of their neck line. Needle two small pointed ear shapes from fawn roving and attach them to the top of the head, upright and close together. Add a small dark-coloured nose tip and needle bead eyes into position.

Work across the body surface with the size-40 needle at a very shallow angle, pulling fine tufts of surface fibre up rather than pressing them down. Work in short passes along the back and sides to suggest the dense, fluffy alpaca fleece. Needle small dark-brown hooves at the foot of each leg. Trim loose fibres around the face with small scissors.

items.problem: The neck bends sideways under the weight of the head
items.cause: The neck core was not firm enough before the head was attached, and the join is too weak to hold upright
items.fix: Needle the neck to a very firm cylinder before attaching. Needle the neck-to-body join from several angles and add more roving at the base if needed.

items.cause: The two front legs are set too far back under the body
items.fix: Position front legs slightly forward of the midline of the body to give a stable forward-back stance.
